title: Dogen's Time and Reality
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: In Soto Zen teachings, Dogen challenges our conventional understanding of time as a linear progression by suggesting that reality and time are intertwined and inseparable. This means that every moment is a complete manifestation of existence, and our actions in each present moment resonate throughout time, affecting past and future. By embracing this non-dualistic understanding through meditation and mindfulness practices like Zazen, we can experience the fluid nature of reality and cultivate a deeper sense of interconnectedness with all things.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the [unclear: "tatakara's"] words.*
Good evening, my friends.
Tonight I would like to share some reflections on the teachings of our great ancestor, Zen master Eihei Dogen.
Particularly, I wanted to scrape the surface of his insights on reality and time.
Dogen's teachings are like a deep well from which we can continue to draw wisdom and inspiration for our practice.
Also, we can get totally lost and drown in the same well and not know what's up, what's down, what's sideways.
With Dogen's language and wording, and his many references to and quotes of ancient Chinese scripture, we sometimes really end up scratching our heads, quite unsure what to think and where to go.
Most of you are very familiar with Dogen Zenchi, or Eihei Dogen.
He lived from 1200 to 1253, and he was a Japanese Buddhist monk who founded the Soto Zen School in Japan.
He's best known for his work Shobogenzo, this fancy little tome here, and it translates into the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
It is a collection of fascicles or essays that explore various aspects of our Buddhist practice and philosophy.
Dogen's teachings are characterized and famous for their poetic depth and philosophical rigor, which offer insights into the nature of reality and the essence of time.
And that's what I want to talk about tonight: reality and time.
I'm using two essays to dive a little bit into it.
One we just worked with for quite a bit, which is Genjokoan.
It was [unclear: "Resula's"] subject for the practice period.
The other one is Uji, a fascicle that is very well known.
It translates into time being.
Interestingly enough, in Japanese it also means sometimes, so it's a very ordinary word in many ways.
I'm going to start with Genjokoan, which is one of Dogen's very famous essays, along with Fukanzasengi and Mountains and Rivers Sutra.
Genjokoan means actualizing the fundamental point.
Or Norman once translated it as the koan of this current moment.
It addresses the nature of reality, our reality.
Dogen begins by stating:
*To study the Buddha way is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things.
When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind, as well as the bodies and minds of others, drop away.
No trace of realization remains.
And this no trace continues endlessly.*
Finally, Dogen invites us to see that reality is not something separate from us.
It is intimately intertwined with our own experience.
To understand reality, we must turn inward and study the self.
This study, however, is not an intellectual exercise.
It needs to be a direct experiential investigation.
When we deeply investigate the self, we realize its empty nature.
In forgetting the self, we become one with myriad things.
In Genjokoan, Dogen addresses the dynamic and interdependent nature of reality.
He writes, *When one side is illuminated, the other is dark.* This statement so well reflects the interplay of various aspects of reality.

Dogen suggests that time is not a linear progression of moments, but rather an intricate dance where each moment is both complete in itself and connected to all other moments that have been or will be.
The present moment contains within it the essence of past and future, revealing the seamless nature of time.
Again, this realization is not static, but dynamic and ever-present.
It is a continuous unfolding, a moment-by-moment actualization of the fundamental point.
In this way, Dogen teaches us that reality is fluid, interdependent, and ever-changing.
Dogen further elaborates on the concept of being time in other parts of his work.
This perspective challenges our conventional understanding of time as a sequence of distinct moments passing by.
Dogen asserts that time and existence are not separate.
Instead, they are one and the same.
To exist means to be time, and to be time is to exist.
Now I'm going to jump into Uji, being time or time being.
Uji opens with these lines:
*An ancient Buddha said, For the time being, stand on top of the highest peak.
For the time being, proceed along the bottom of the deepest ocean.
For the time being, three heads and eight arms of a fighting demon.
For the time being, an eight or 16 foot body of the Buddha.
For the time being, a staff or whisk.
For the time being, a pillar or lantern.
For the time being, the children of common families, Zhang and Li.
For the time being, the earth and the sky.
For the time being, here, means time itself is being.
And all being is time.
The golden 16 foot body is time.
Because it is time, there is a radiant illumination of time.*
*Study it as the 12 hours of the present.
Three heads and eight arms is time.
Because it is time, it is not separate from the 12 hours of the present.
Even though you do not measure the hours of the day as long or short, far or near, you still call it 12 hours.
Because the signs of times coming and going are obvious, people do not doubt it.
Although they do not doubt it, they do not understand it.*
End quote.
This is how Uji, for the time being, starts.
Dogen's exploration of time is articulated in Uji.
I do not pretend that I understand a big portion of it.
I've just been nibbling away at its edges.
So, the concept of Uji, being time or sometimes.
This essay demonstrates the idea that time and existence are not separate entities, but are inherently interconnected.
Here, Dogen presents a radical rethinking of time, suggesting its interconnection.
*Time itself is being and all being is time.
The golden 16 foot body is time.
Because it is time, there is the radiance of time.
We should learn that because it is time, it is not separate from time.*
This statement suggests that every moment of time is a complete manifestation of existence.
Time is not something that flows independently of beings.
Rather, every being is a manifestation of time.
Each moment is a full expression of reality, embodying the totality of existence.
In Dogen's view, every moment is complete in itself and nothing is lacking.
And each something that unfolds in time is time itself.
This means that our existence unfolds in time and is time itself.
Past, present and future are not linear segments, but are all part of the present moment's complete reality.
By fully immersing ourselves in each moment, we can actualize our true nature and realize the timeless essence of our being.
I'm going to loop back briefly, because one of Dogen's most radical departures from conventional thought is his rejection of the linear conception of time.
In our modern world, we go by the clock, we go by the watch.
We perceive time as past, present and future.
Dogen kind of throws that out of the window.
He presents a different perspective: *The way the self [unclear: "erase itself"] is the form of the entire world.
See each thing in this entire world as a moment of time.* I'll repeat this point because it really doesn't fit into our cause and effect thinking.
According to Dogen, each thing, each being and each moment is a total embodiment of time.
This perspective invites us to see that time is not a series of disconnected points, but an interdependent reality.
Every moment contains within it all other moments, past, present and future.
In this view, each moment is both unique and complete in itself, and also intrinsically linked to every other moment.
This means that our actions in this present moment resonate throughout time, affecting past and future.
This interconnectedness challenges us to live each moment fully, recognizing that it is a complete expression of our being.
Dogen emphasizes the interdependence of all moments in Uji: *Real existence is only this exact moment.
All moments of time being, of being time, are the whole of time.
And all existent things and all existent phenomena are time.*
I would like to read you from the Treasury of the True Dharma.
In the foreword there's this really great quote that fits into this.
It's called Beyond Space and Time, and it's a rather long quote.
*The distance from here to there is no longer concrete.
A meditator walks on the top of a high mountain and swims deep in the ocean, not only becoming an awakened one, but also identifying with a fighting spirit.
A person who bows becomes one with the person who is bowed to.
Sizes become free of sizes.
The depth of a dewdrop is the height of the moon.
The entire world is found in a minute particle.
Extremely large becomes extremely small and vice versa.
Here is another view of reality distinct from our usual way of seeing.
It is not that duality stops existing or functioning.
The small is still small and the large is still large.
The body remains the body and the mind remains the mind.
Without discerning the differences between things, we could not conduct even the simplest task of our daily lives.
And yet, in meditation, the distinctions seem to dissolve and lose their usual significance.
Dogen calls this kind of non-dualistic experience nirvana, which exists at each moment of meditation.*
*Dogen is perhaps the only Zen master in the ancient world who elucidated in detail the paradox of time.
For him, time is not separate from existence.
Time is being.
Certainly, there is a passage of time marked by the movement of the sun or the clock that always manifests in one direction from the past to the present to the future.
On the other hand, in some cases we feel that time flies and in other cases it moves slowly or almost then still.
In meditation, according to Dogen, time is multi-directional.
Yesterday flows into today and today flows into yesterday.
Today flows into tomorrow and tomorrow flows into today.
Today also flows into today.
Time flies, yet it does not fly away.
This moment, which is inclusive of all times, is timeless.
Further, time is not apart from the one who experiences it.
Time is the Self.
Time flows in I, and I makes the time flow.
It is selfless I that makes time full and complete.*
So you might say this is all kind of theoretical.
What do I do with this?
How can we bring that into our practice?
Here are a few thoughts that you might want to take up, or probably not.
Zazen.
In Zazen, we sit and we simply are.
We allow ourselves to experience the fullness of each moment, letting go of attachments to past and future.
This can help us to embody this teaching of being time, where each moment of Zazen is complete and whole in itself.
The other one can be mindfulness in daily life.
As we go about our daily activities, we can bring mindful awareness to each task, no matter how mundane.
By fully engaging with what we're doing, we can experience the interconnectedness of all things and the fluid nature of reality.
And of course, with time comes up the thought of impermanence.
As we go about our daily lives, we can observe that everything is constantly changing.
If we embrace impermanence, we can let go of some of the clinging, some of the aversion, opening ourselves to the flow of life with grace and equanimity.
Of course, the question of time and the question of reality are around us all the time.
We can engage in this deep inquiry into our own nature, into our own being time.
Who or what are we beyond our thoughts and feelings?
What is the true nature of our existence?
Thank you very much.
*[unclear: "I don't make it so boundless"].
I vow to enter there.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I want to become it.*
